topic: planning a multi-day kayak trip through a lake chain with portages

provenance.author: glowny-en-c
provenance.notes: 10 turns, user first; variant a is a distance, food and cost sheet for the same loop with closed task questions, base is a planning talk about managing three portages. Grounded external referent: the portage cart, introduced in turn 0 (it wobbles under one boat) and mentioned in the sentence directly before every insertion (bolts, garden test, wheels, the rutted path).

a: The kayak trip needs a distance sheet and the paddling legs come first on it.
Day one covers twelve kilometres and day two covers fifteen kilometres on open water.
Day three covers nine kilometres and day four covers fourteen on the river arm.
Day five covers ten kilometres back along the south shore to the landing stage.
How many kilometres of paddling does the whole loop come to in one figure?
base: We are planning a five day kayak loop through the lake chain north of the town.
Three portages link the lakes, and the longest one runs nearly two kilometres uphill.
Our folding cart is meant to carry one boat and it wobbles with any real load.
There are two of us with two loaded boats and food for the whole five days.
How should we plan the carries so the long portage does not break the trip?

a: The paddling comes to sixty kilometres across the five days in one round figure.
Now add the three portages of one, two, and one and a half kilometres.
Every portage is walked three times over, first the boats and then the bags.
Work out the total walking distance that the three portages add to the trip.
Which single portage adds the most walking on the three crossings rule?
base: Plan every portage as two carries each, and the long one will lose its teeth.
Take the boats over first with the cart, then walk back for the bags together.
A cart that wobbles under one boat should never be asked to take two at once.
Tighten the cart frame bolts and wrap the axle ends with tape before you leave.
How heavy is each boat once the hatches are packed for five days out?

a: The two kilometre portage adds six kilometres of walking on the three crossings rule.
The other two portages add three and four and a half kilometres of walking.
Give the full walking figure and then the trip figure with paddling counted in.
Round nothing yet, and keep the halves in the figures as they stand.
Does the whole trip pass seventy kilometres once the walking goes in?
base: Each boat comes to about thirty kilograms once the hatches are packed and closed.
The food barrel adds twelve kilograms on day one and lightens as we eat.
The cart took one packed boat around the garden without folding, after the bolt work.
The cart's little wheels sank into the soft lawn, and the portage paths may be softer still.
Would wider wheels be worth the money this close to the leaving date?

a: The trip comes to seventy-three and a half kilometres with the walking counted in.
Now build the food sheet at two people and five days on the water.
Breakfast and supper come from the barrel and lunch rides in the day bags.
Count ten barrel meals and ten bag lunches for the pair across the trip.
How many meals in all does the food sheet carry for the two of you?
base: Wider wheels are the single best money this trip can spend before the off.
Soft path plus narrow wheel equals a plough, and you will drag rather than roll.
Fit the cart with the widest wheels its axle takes and test it fully loaded.
Strap the boat at the cockpit rim and at the stern handle, never just amidships.
Have you walked the long portage empty, or is it new ground for you both?

a: The food sheet carries twenty meals in all for the two of you.
One correction from the outfitter before the sheet is printed for the barrel.
The trip runs six days on the water, not five as first written down.
Rework the paddling and the meals with day six at eight kilometres.
What are the new paddling figure and the new meal count for the sheet?
base: The long portage is new ground for both of us, found only on the map sheet.
The map shows a steady climb through spruce with one marked boggy dip halfway.
A club note says the cart path is clear but rutted after the spring rains.
We can reach the trailhead by road on Sunday and walk it with empty hands.
Is a Sunday walk through worth the fuel and the lost packing afternoon?

a: The paddling figure moves to sixty-eight kilometres with day six set at eight kilometres.
The meal count moves to twenty-four at two more barrel meals and two more lunches.
The walking stays at thirteen and a half kilometres on the three crossings rule.
Now give the new whole trip figure with the paddling and the walking added together.
Does the barrel hold twelve meals when the two extra barrel meals go in?
base: Walk it, since one seen bog beats ten imagined ones, and Sunday buys you that sight.
Mark the dip with a stick count so you know it again under a loaded cart.
Time the empty walk, then double it for the first loaded crossing in your plan.
If the ruts run deeper than a fist, plan the bags for backs not wheels.
Would your knees take the bags on backs if the ruts turn out fist deep?

a: The whole trip figure is eighty-one and a half kilometres as the sheet stands.
The barrel holds twelve meals with the two extra barrel meals counted in.
Now set the camp list with five nights numbered along the loop.
Night three follows the long portage and night five sits by the landing.
Which night number falls at the far end of the long portage?
base: Our knees are fine with bags, and we carried packs over this range years ago.
Sunday is agreed, and the stick count for the bog made us both laugh.
Camp two sits at the far end of the long portage by the map.
Arriving there spent, with wet boots, is my honest worry for that day.
Should we move camp two closer and split the long portage across two days?

a: Night three falls at the far end of the long portage on the present list.
Move night three to the near side and put the crossing on the next morning.
Renumber the five nights and keep the last night by the landing as it was.
The day six paddling of eight kilometres stands unchanged after the camp move.
Which day now carries the long portage crossing on the reworked camp list?
base: Split it, so one day ends at the near side and you cross fresh the next morning.
A morning crossing gives you dry boots by noon and a camp set in daylight.
The near side clearing on the map looks flat enough for two small tents.
Water is the one thing to check there, since the stream may run dry by August.
Do your barrels carry enough water for a dry camp if it comes to that?

a: Day four now carries the long portage crossing on the reworked morning list.
Set the water line at six litres spare across the two food barrels together.
Add the wheel set at thirty pounds to the cost sheet for the cart.
The cost sheet already holds maps at twelve pounds and fees at twenty.
Close out the cost sheet with one figure across the three lines added together.
base: The barrels carry six litres spare, and we will top up at the last spring.
The near side camp is agreed, and the morning crossing suits us both well.
My partner will book the Sunday walk and check the club note again for changes.
We leave in nine days, and the packing list is the last big job now.
The wide wheels arrive midweek, which leaves one evening for fitting and a test.

a: The cost sheet closes at sixty-two pounds across wheels, maps, and fees.
The trip sheet closes at eighty-one and a half kilometres over six days.
The meal sheet closes at twenty-four meals with twelve riding in the barrel.
The camp list closes at five nights with night three on the near side.
Every sheet now carries a closing figure and the plan is ready to print.
base: Nine days is comfortable if the wheels fit midweek and the Sunday walk holds.
Load the cart for the test exactly as it will be loaded on the long portage.
Walk it round the block twice, once uphill, and listen for the frame creaking.
Pack the barrel last so the heavy meals ride low and the bread rides high.
A trip planned to this depth usually gives back an easy first morning.

insertions.neutral: Funny how the route drawn on the map never shows which turns it dropped.
